passages.t: Rejoice in the Lord, and a warning
passages.happening:
“Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord. It is no trouble for me to write the same things to you again, and it is a safeguard for you” (verse 1).

Then the tone turns sharp: “Watch out for those dogs, those workers of evil, those mutilators of the flesh!” (verse 2).

Paul gives the reason: “For it is we who are the circumcision, we who worship by the Spirit of God, who glory in Christ Jesus, and who put no confidence in the flesh” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
Paul does not name the people he warns against, but what he says makes their teaching clear. They taught that Gentile believers in Jesus had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to belong fully to God's people. Teachers like this had troubled Paul's churches in Galatia (Galatians 2 and 5), and the apostles had met in Jerusalem and agreed that Gentile believers did not need to be circumcised (Acts 15). There is no sign these teachers had reached Philippi yet. Paul may be warning the church before they arrive.

In that world dogs were mostly scavengers in the streets, not pets, and ‘dogs’ was a common insult for people thought unclean or outside. Paul turns the insult around: the ones who want to shut Gentiles out are behaving like the outsiders.

He also makes a sharp play on words. The Greek for circumcision is peritomē. He calls these teachers the katatomē, ‘the mutilation’, a cutting that only cuts. Then he says that believers in Jesus, Jews and Gentiles together, are ‘the circumcision’: the people marked out for God, not by a cut in the body, but by the Spirit, by joy in Christ, and by not trusting in themselves.

And notice who is speaking. The next verses show that Paul is a Jew, proud of his people, circumcised himself.
passages.ot:
The idea of a circumcised heart is not Paul's invention. It runs through the law and the prophets. Moses said, “Circumcise your hearts, therefore, and stiffen your necks no more” (Deuteronomy 10:16), and promised, “The LORD your God will circumcise your hearts and the hearts of your descendants, and you will love Him with all your heart and with all your soul, so that you may live” (Deuteronomy 30:6). Jeremiah called out, “Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and remove the foreskins of your hearts” (Jeremiah 4:4).

So when Paul says that true circumcision is worship by the Spirit, he is standing inside Israel's own Scriptures.
passages.hard:
Paul calls these teachers ‘dogs’ and ‘mutilators of the flesh’. Is this a word against the Jewish people?

No. This was a dispute among believers in Jesus about whether Gentile converts had to be circumcised. Paul is a Jew, as he says in the next verses: ‘circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin; a Hebrew of Hebrews’ (verse 5). Elsewhere he says he would give up his own salvation for his people (Romans 9:3), and asks, ‘did God reject His people?’ and answers that he did not (Romans 11:1). His harsh words are aimed at a teaching that, in his judgment, added a condition to God's grace, not at Jews, not at Judaism, and not at circumcision as God gave it to Abraham.

For centuries some Christians used words like these to justify contempt for Jews. That reading is false, and this site rejects it. The note on Acts 2:22-28 says why.

As with Galatians 5:12, the Bible records Paul's sharp words honestly. It does not ask us to copy them. They are no pattern for how believers speak to or about anyone.
passages.asks: Paul says the people of God are marked by worship in the Spirit, joy in Christ, and no confidence in themselves. Ask what you add to Christ to feel sure of your place with God: a record, a church, a tradition, a good week. And ask whether you have ever made others meet conditions God did not set.

passages.t: Everything counted as loss, to gain Christ
passages.happening:
If anyone could trust in his own record, Paul says, he could. “I have more: circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin; a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee; as to zeal, persecuting the church; as to righteousness in the law, faultless” (verses 4-6).

“But whatever was gain to me I count as loss for the sake of Christ” (verse 7). “I count all things as loss compared to the surpassing excellence of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (verse 8). He wants to “be found in Him, not having my own righteousness from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God on the basis of faith” (verse 9).

“I want to know Christ and the power of His resurrection and the fellowship of His sufferings, being conformed to Him in His death, and so, somehow, to attain to the resurrection from the dead” (verses 10-11).
passages.hearers:
Paul's list has seven items. The first four he was born with: circumcised on the eighth day as the law said, an Israelite, of the tribe of Benjamin, the tribe of Israel's first king, Saul, whose name Paul also bore, and a Hebrew born of Hebrews. The last three he achieved: a Pharisee, one of the most respected and careful keepers of the law; so zealous that he persecuted the church; and ‘faultless’ in keeping the law. That last word does not mean he never sinned. It means his public record of keeping the law was spotless.

Then comes the turn, in the language of bookkeeping. ‘Gain’ and ‘loss’ were words for the two columns of an account. Paul moves everything he was proud of into the loss column. Not because his people or the law were bad. Because, set beside Christ, they could not be what he trusted in.

‘Rubbish’ in verse 8 is a deliberately coarse word in Greek, used for scraps thrown out or worse. Paul chooses a word that shocks.

Notice the shape. It is the shape of the song in chapter 2. Christ did not hold on to his equality with God; Paul does not hold on to his record. Christ went down to death and was raised; Paul wants to share Christ's sufferings and his resurrection.
passages.ot:
Paul's pride in his birth was not foolish; these were real gifts. Circumcision on the eighth day was God's command to Abraham: “every male must be circumcised when he is eight days old” (Genesis 17:12). Benjamin's tribe gave Israel its first king. Kish was “a Benjamite”, and “he had a son named Saul” (1 Samuel 9:1-2).

But the prophets already knew that no human record can stand before God on its own. “Each of us has become like something unclean, and all our righteous acts are like filthy rags” (Isaiah 64:6). And Habakkuk said, “the righteous will live by faith” (Habakkuk 2:4).

The hope of resurrection is in Daniel: “many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life” (Daniel 12:2).
passages.hard:
Verse 9 speaks of righteousness ‘through faith in Christ’. Some Bibles and readers take the Greek differently. What is the question?

The Greek phrase can be read ‘faith in Christ’, as the BSB has it, or ‘the faith’ or ‘faithfulness of Christ’. The same question comes up in Romans 3 and Galatians 2. On the first reading, righteousness is received by trusting Christ. On the second, it rests on Christ's own faithful obedience, all the way to the cross, and the next words, ‘on the basis of faith’, speak of our trust. These notes do not choose, as the site's chapter note on Philippians 3 does not. Both readings agree that righteousness comes from God, not from the law, and both put Christ at the centre. The question is how Paul said it, not whether salvation is by grace.

And what does ‘somehow, to attain to the resurrection’ (verse 11) mean? It is not doubt about whether God will raise him. Paul is humble about the way, which runs through suffering and death, and certain of the end. The next verses say he has not yet arrived.
passages.asks: Paul made a list of everything he once trusted. Try making yours: your background, your achievements, your good record, your church. Ask which of them you lean on to feel right with God. And ask what it would mean to count them as loss next to knowing Christ, not because they are bad, but because he is better.

passages.happening:
“Not that I have already obtained all this, or have already been made perfect, but I press on to take hold of that for which Christ Jesus took hold of me” (verse 12).

“Brothers, I do not consider myself yet to have taken hold of it. But one thing I do: Forgetting what is behind and straining toward what is ahead, I press on toward the goal to win the prize of God’s heavenly calling in Christ Jesus” (verses 13-14).

Those who are mature should think this way, and if anyone thinks differently, God will make it clear (verse 15). “Nevertheless, we must live up to what we have already attained” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The picture is a race, the kind run in stadiums across the Greek world. A runner does not look back over his shoulder. He leans forward, straining toward the finish line, where a prize waits.

Paul, the great apostle, says he has not arrived. He is not yet perfect. That must have surprised some readers. It still surprises some. The Christian life is not a matter of having made it, but of running.

And look at verse 12. Paul presses on to take hold of Christ ‘because’ Christ first took hold of him. The race begins with being caught by Christ. Everything Paul does is a response to being grabbed by grace on the road to Damascus.

‘Forgetting what is behind’ does not mean pretending the past did not happen. Paul has just listed his past. It means not living in it, neither in old successes nor in old failures. For Paul those included the church he once persecuted. He does not let either his pride or his guilt hold him back.
passages.ot:
The prophets pictured God's people given strength for a long race: “But those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength; they will mount up with wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary, they will walk and not faint” (Isaiah 40:31).

And the Psalms show the same longing that moves Paul toward the goal: “As the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul longs after You, O God” (Psalm 42:1).
passages.asks: Paul says he has not arrived. Ask whether you have quietly decided that you have. Ask what lies behind you that you keep looking back at: an old success you live on, or an old failure you cannot put down. And ask what one step toward Christ you could take this week.

passages.t: Enemies of the cross, and citizens of heaven
passages.happening:
“Join one another in following my example, brothers, and carefully observe those who walk according to the pattern we set for you” (verse 17).

“For as I have often told you before, and now say again even with tears: Many live as enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame. Their minds are set on earthly things” (verses 18-19).

“But our citizenship is in heaven, and we eagerly await a Savior from there, the Lord Jesus Christ, who, by the power that enables Him to subject all things to Himself, will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body” (verses 20-21).
passages.hearers:
‘Follow my example’ can sound proud. But Paul has just said he has not arrived. He means: follow the direction I am running, and watch others who run the same way.

Who are the ‘enemies of the cross’? Paul does not say, and readers differ. Some think they are the same teachers as in verse 2, with ‘belly’ meaning food laws and ‘shame’ meaning circumcision. Others think they are people in the churches who treated freedom in Christ as permission to live for their appetites. Either way, notice two things. Paul speaks of them ‘with tears’, not with a sneer. And the problem he names is a life ruled by appetite and set on earthly things, the opposite of the mind of Christ in chapter 2.

Then verse 20. Philippi was a Roman colony. Its citizens were proud that, though they lived far away, they belonged to Rome, and they looked to the emperor, often hailed as saviour, to protect them. Paul says believers belong to another city. Their true homeland is heaven, and the Saviour they wait for is not the emperor but Jesus.

And what Jesus will do is not take them away from their bodies, but change them. ‘Our lowly bodies’ will be made like his risen body. The Christian hope is resurrection.
passages.ot:
Daniel promised that the dead would rise (Daniel 12:2), and the Psalms looked beyond the grave to God himself: “But God will redeem my life from Sheol, for He will surely take me to Himself” (Psalm 49:15). “As for me, I will behold Your face in righteousness; when I awake, I will be satisfied in Your presence” (Psalm 17:15).

And God's people had lived as citizens of one kingdom inside another before. To the exiles in Babylon God said, “Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles. Pray to the LORD on its behalf” (Jeremiah 29:7). Belonging to God never meant despising the place where you live.
passages.hard:
What does ‘our citizenship is in heaven’ mean for how believers live in their own country?

It does not mean believers should not care about the world, or should escape from it. Paul expects them to stay in Philippi, work, raise families and do good to their neighbours. Jeremiah told God's people to seek the good of the city where they lived.

But it does mean that no earthly country is their first loyalty. Paul wrote to people proud of being Roman, and told them that Rome was not their true home and Caesar was not their Saviour. The same word speaks to believers in every country now. Any teaching that makes a nation God's chosen kingdom, or ties the gospel to one flag or party, puts an earthly citizenship where the heavenly one belongs. That is an error, whoever makes it, and the cross belongs to no flag.

And it gives no one leave for contempt. Paul names the ‘enemies of the cross’ with tears. Believers who hold their earthly loyalties loosely are free to love their neighbours, whoever they are.
passages.asks: Paul says your citizenship is in heaven. Ask which loyalty shapes your opinions most: Christ, or a country, a party or a group. Ask what your mind is set on. And ask whether you speak of people you think are wrong with tears, as Paul did, or with a sneer.
